title: Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'
description: Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who
body: Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who are negatively affected on a daily basis.Pegg said he had previously been putting his symptoms down to "just character fault".The actor and writer also spoke about his mental health, including having clinical depression and struggling to control his drinking, which he said he initially thought had "caused" his diagnosis."I felt like it was something that had come on in later life because I wasn't a naughty child."I've had bouts of depression in my adult life since 18 and I thought maybe it had come on with that."Maybe over the years with therapy and medication - whatever - I've been treating the symptoms and not the cause of why I feel that way."Pegg said: "I did feel different in a way I might not be able to put my finger on. Maybe everybody feels that way."I just assumed ADHD kids were kind of chaotic and difficult and didn't pay attention in school," he added."But there were other things that I did do as a kid – fidget or whatever – that made me think, 'Oh no, maybe I've had this longer than I thought'."Pegg said his wife has been supportive and is "dealing with it as if I'd been diagnosed ages ago", adding: "It's just who I am, and it's just things that I do."She makes allowances for forgetfulness and and lack of concentration."Other celebrities who have been diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood include comedian and actor Johnny Vegas, comic and presenter Sue Perkins, presenters Ant McPartlin and Richard Bacon, comedian Rory Bremner and model Erin O'Connor.ADHD is described by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) as "a behavioural syndrome characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention".The NHS estimates that about 2.5 million people in England have ADHD, including those without a formal diagnosis.Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand.Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018.Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest ADHD is actually underdiagnosed.In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.

schema.headline: Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'

title: Anne Carson: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet wins Nobel Prize in Literature
description: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that oft
body: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement. "She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said."She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."

schema.headline: Anne Carson: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet wins Nobel Prize in Literature

title: Hate crime figures rise after more offences motivated by religion and race, figures show
description: "We are delivering the biggest reforms to policing in over 200 years, alongside record funding to protect Muslim and Jewish people and places of worsh
body: "We are delivering the biggest reforms to policing in over 200 years, alongside record funding to protect Muslim and Jewish people and places of worship," she added.The Home Office said there were a total of 146,825 hate crimes recorded by police in the two nations in the year to March 2026.Racially-motivated offences accounted for the majority of all police recorded hate crimes, at around 74%, with about 8% of other hate crimes classified as religious.The Home Office said the rise in these offences over the last year was due to an increase in public order offences, often taking the form of intimidation and abuse, but crimes involving violence and vandalism were also included in the statistics."In the last two years, there has been a rise in hate crime offences that is not seen in the overall violent and public order offences trend," the report said."This may suggest there has been a genuine increase in hate crime offences over the last two years."Where the ethnicity of the victim was known in the race and religion related hate crimes, around one third of victims were identified as Asian and around a quarter as black.The Home Office said that it was likely that hate crime "offences against white victims will include xenophobic abuse against people not born in the UK".The figures showed a 13% rise in religious hate crimes recorded by police during the year to March 2026, with 11,419 recorded offences in total.Of those there was a 15% rise in hate crimes targeting Muslims and 10% increase in those that targeted Jewish people.The increase in hate crimes targeting Muslims (from 4,479 to 5,132 offences) showed a particular rise in September of last year, which the Home Office said "coincided with a number of protests and incidents of public order".There were hate crimes targeting both Muslims and Jewish people following the start of the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel in the spring of this year.Antisemitic hate crimes have been at elevated levels since the beginning of the conflict between Israel and Hamas in 2023, but saw a spike in October 2025 following the fatal attack at the Heaton Park Synagogue in Manchester.Other attacks followed in the months after, including in March when four Jewish community ambulances were torched in Golders Green, north London. Prosecutors say the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.Additional reporting by Robert Cuffe

schema.headline: Hate crime figures rise after more offences motivated by religion and race, figures show

title: 'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows
description: There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders.The warning comes as new
body: There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders.The warning comes as new data reveals the waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row.An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.The numbers are the highest since October 2025 and have raised questions over whether the NHS will meet a government target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.The rise in waiting lists comes despite the NHS in England delivering what were described as record levels of planned, elective care over the summer, while demand for services also reached its highest level ever.A record 4.7 million planned treatments, procedures and appointments occurred across June, July and August – more than in any previous summer.But both A&Es and ambulance services also saw a record number of patients for the month of September.NHS England's national medical director, Professor Frankie Swords, warned that despite the progress delivered by frontline teams, winter pressure was already building."Staff are already seeing the ominous early signs of pressure, with more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year, and unfortunately many people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she said.The NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, says the government in England is not going to achieve its manifesto promise of hitting the 18-week hospital waiting time target by the end of the parliament in 2029.That 18-week target hasn't been hit for a decade.A separate analysis by the Health Foundation think-tank said progress on cutting waiting times had stalled over the past year, with referrals on to the waiting list rising at a much quicker rate than the number of patients being treated.Sir Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance which represents NHS trusts, said: "The NHS continues to respond to record demand for care, but the relentless growth in demand for services is putting NHS staff under real pressure."Francesca Cavallaro, of the Health Foundation, said: "Thanks to the hard work of staff, the NHS has made progress in bringing down waiting times, but a rise in referrals mean that the service is having to run faster just to stand still and the prospects of meeting the government's pledge are receding."Andy Burnham's government have yet to set out whether they will give the 18-week target the same priority as it had under Keir Starmer, but our analysis shows the pledge is becoming increasingly hard to deliver."There will be concern too that the pressures of a long, hot summer have merged almost seamlessly into the pressures associated with the winter months. More patients, including children, have been arriving at A&E departments with flu and other respiratory viruses.The number of patients seen within four hours in A&Es last month fell to 74.4%,  down from 75.0% in August.The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted – what is known as "corridor care" – stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.That has alarmed Dr Vicky Price, president of the Society for Acute Medicine."A 13% year-on-year rise in 12-hour emergency department waits as winter approaches should set alarm bells ringing. "More than 50,000 patients waited over 12 hours from the decision to admit to admission in September - 1,686 people every day. "These are not just numbers."They represent vulnerable people who are waiting far too long for a bed and staff trying to deliver safe care in overcrowded emergency departments."The government says the 18-week mark could still be achieved, saying it was investing in NHS buildings and equipment to make services more productive.It also pointed to disruption to care that was caused by the strikes by resident doctors, a dispute which has now been settled.But the strain that services are feeling in September, before winter has even really got going, will be a cause for concern among NHS leaders and their political bosses alike.

schema.headline: 'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows

title: 'Asos hacked': What can I do to protect myself?
description: Image caption, The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on TuesdayByJemma CrewBusine
body: Image caption, The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on TuesdayByJemma CrewBusiness reporter and Laura CressTechnology reporterUpdated 15 minutes agoIf a strange-looking message from Asos popped up on your phone on Tuesday, you may be worrying what it could mean and whether you need to do anything. The online retailer has emailed customers apologising for the "unauthorised push notification" containing an external link, adding that they should disregard the message and not click on it.Here's what has happened, and what those who may have been affected are being advised to do.What message did people receive?On Tuesday morning, Asos users across the UK were sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company."Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message read.Later that day, Asos said it took immediate action to restrict the apparent hackers' access, was investigating and working with advisers and relevant authorities on "next steps".Data storage company Snowflake told the BBC its investigations had "found no compromise" of its platform.On Wednesday the cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, got in contact with the BBC and claimed they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.Simon AI has been contacted for comment.What does this mean for my data?On Thursday Asos told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals.Search terms used by customers - like  "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" - are also visible in the data.In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".What can I do to protect myself?For now, the advice is:Don't click the link: The hack notification included a link to a Telegram account - Asos and cyber security experts say not to click on itChange passwords: It's worth updating your password, including across other sites that use the same one as your Asos account. The advice for a strong password is to mix numbers, symbols and upper and lower case characters, and avoid using the same password across multiple accountsTurn on two-step verification for important apps like banking and email: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls this "one of the most effective ways to protect your online accounts from cyber criminals". You can usually turn it on by going into the security settings in your accountMonitor transactions: Keep an eye on your online transactions for anything unusualPaul Arnold, Chief Executive of the Information Commission's Office (ICO) said if customers do change their passwords, they must ensure they log in to their account "directly through the official website or app" and update it in the usual way.Be alert going forwardAccording to Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at global cyber-security firm Check Point, "the biggest immediate risk may be what happens next". She said criminals know people will be searching for information online and expects there to be "attempts to exploit that confusion". Her advice to Asos customers is not to be "scared and frightened". But she said they should be "extremely suspicious" of emails, texts or messages claiming their account has been compromised, offering a refund or asking them to click a link to reset their password.People should hang up the phone if they receive any calls from someone they think might be posing as Asos or another organisation, said Which? spokesperson Kat Cereda. The consumer rights expert said they should contact the organisation themselves afterwards through separate means.Dr Richard Horne, CEO of the NCSC, agreed that customers should "stay vigilant to suspicious messages that may seek to take advantage of news of the breach".The NCSC website, external says these could include "official-sounding messages about 'resetting passwords', 'receiving compensation', 'scanning devices' or 'missed deliveries'".Unanswered questionsSeveral questions remain unanswered.It isn't yet clear who exactly is behind the message, although we know the group calls itself Xuanyewen.And we don't know how many people received the notification or how many may be impacted.Anastasia Tikhonova, Global Head of Threat Research at the cybersecurity firm Group-IB said the group behind the message was "a newly surfaced name"."Its Telegram channel was created on the day the message went out," she said. "That tells us when it became visible, not when anyone got in or who is behind it." Asos said its website and app were operating "as normal, and customers can continue to shop with confidence on ASOS as normal" as of Tuesday night.It said protecting customers "is our priority", and it will provide a further update "as soon as we have confirmed more information". People should visit Asos's official website directly for updates.

schema.headline: 'Asos hacked': What can I do to protect myself?

title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
description: Image source, ReutersByHenri AstierSince late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have
body: Image source, ReutersByHenri AstierSince late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds."Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 19:00, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.Figure caption, Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on TuesdayThose grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.Image source, EPAImage caption, About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages.  It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.Figure caption, Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters?Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.The street does not always win.In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BFMTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse stringsThe government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

schema.headline: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger

title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
description: Figure caption, Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the pastByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsThe UK
body: Figure caption, Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the pastByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsThe UK needs to do more to back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market, are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.'Take the handbrake off'"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast."We need to take the handbrake off." The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange,  travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.'Stop throwing shade'Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns."We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said."We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit." Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia HoggettThe boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list.However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax, external Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month."As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.

schema.headline: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK

title: UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham on Berlin trip
description: Image source, AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Burnham is meeting Chancellor Friedrich Merz on his first official visit to GermanyByEwan Somerville
body: Image source, AFP/Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Burnham is meeting Chancellor Friedrich Merz on his first official visit to GermanyByEwan SomervillePolitical reporterJennifer McKiernanPolitical reporter and Jessica ParkerBerlin correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoThe UK and Germany will face threats together, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said as he reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships.On his first official European trip, apart from visits to Ukraine, Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and was greeted with military honours in Berlin.Speaking to reporters at the German capital's Federal Chancellery, the prime minister said both countries were facing hybrid attacks "on a regular basis" and "it makes sense" to take them on together.The pair formally ratified the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity.Burnham said the treaty would "improve our security here in Europe" but also help grow the economy and living standards.He added that the UK government would now "seek to progress" Germany joining Gcap, the Global Combat Air Programme led by Italy, Japan and the UK to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft. He outlined partnerships "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".He mentioned collaboration on quantum technology and space, adding he was aiming to host the first joint meeting of the UK and German cabinets next year.The Berlin talks come after intelligence services warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.Image source, Bloomberg/Getty ImagesImage caption, The meeting was held at the Chancellery building in BerlinMeanwhile, French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the European Union, in an interview with the BBC's economics editor Faisal Islam.Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was "very committed to securing deeper cooperation" and to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe". He told reporters a closer relationship with Europe was in the interests of growth and tackling irregular migration. In recent weeks he has mentioned the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.The German leader replied: "From our German side, I can assure you that we will do anything what we can do to bring the UK closer and closer back to Europe, to the European continent, to the European Union."The meeting comes as European leaders have been warning that the threat of hybrid attacks against Europe by Russia has intensified.Hybrid attacks can include potentially destabilising activity such as cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation.Sir Mark Lyall Grant, former UK national security adviser, explained that hybrid warfare "falls somewhere between peace and war - it's in that sort of grey zone, an area where Russia has been extremely active for some time".He told Radio 4's Today that while Russia had posed a threat to the UK since Vladimir Putin became president in 2001, there had been an "intensification" in response to European support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion."We know Russia has been mapping undersea cables in the North Sea; that's something I'm sure Andy Burnham will be talking to Chancellor Merz about because it affects both the UK and Germany," he added.Last month, a senior Russian diplomat was summoned by the British government over an "egregious and reckless attack" on Leipzig airport, while the EU's foreign affairs chief also summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham was greeted with German military honoursIt is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.Meanwhile, questions have been raised this week about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage.The talks also come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny. Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory. Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections.Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.Additional reporting by Ottilie Mitchell.Get in touchDo you have any comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham on Berlin trip

title: Husband accused of Norfolk GP murder appears at Crown Court
description: The husband of a GP who was found dead at her home has appeared before a Crown Court, charged with her murder.The body of 45-year-old Hannah Cain, kno
body: The husband of a GP who was found dead at her home has appeared before a Crown Court, charged with her murder.The body of 45-year-old Hannah Cain, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday.Mark Cain, 45, also of Fern Hill, was charged with murder on Tuesday.Appearing via video link from HMP Norwich, he spoke only to confirm his name and that he understood proceedings at King's Lynn Crown Court. He was remanded in custody until a plea hearing on 3 December.Steven Ball, prosecuting, said Mark Cain was accused of the murder of his wife on 3 October into the early hours of 4 October at their family home.He said emergency services attended and Hannah Cain was found "unconscious and unresponsive".A post-mortem examination recorded that she had sustained "blunt force injuries to the head" and "neck injuries consistent with compression to the neck", he said.

schema.headline: Husband accused of Norfolk GP murder appears at Crown Court

title: Stabbed Norwich schoolgirl went into 'panic mode', court told
description: Image source, ContributedImage caption, A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the sceneByRobby Westat King's Lynn  C
body: Image source, ContributedImage caption, A photo taken from within a classroom showed an armed police officer at the sceneByRobby Westat King's Lynn  Crown CourtA schoolgirl who was stabbed by a masked fellow pupil at school described how "everything was going numb" and she had "blood all over her hands", a court has been told.Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back.The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.In a police interview played to the court, the girl described how she went into "panic mode" after being stabbed, King's Lynn Crown Court heard.Image source, Shaun Whitmore/BBCImage caption, Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School at 10:24 GMT on 11 MarchShe told officers: "He was standing there head to toe in black, no school uniform whatsoever."Describing the attack, which took place in a corridor, she said it felt like she had been punched and then shortly afterwards felt a "sharp pain shoot through my back".When she realised she had been stabbed, she said: "I was in panic mode. Everything was going numb and feeling weak."She said there was "blood all over my hands" and described how police had to cut off her clothes to access the wound.When asked during the interview, which was conducted shortly after the incident, how she was feeling, the girl said: "A bit in shock, think it will hit me eventually, but it hasn't yet."She told officers she did not know the attacker and did not have any issues with people at school.Whilst giving evidence, the girl, who cannot be named because of her age, broke down in tears.Image source, Qays Najm/BBCImage caption, The trial at King's Lynn Crown Court is expected to last three weeksThe court has already been told that the defendant had written notes saying he hated women.One note, which prosecutors said was found by police pinned to the wall of his bedroom, said: "My barren world.. Hello. To all readers out there in the UK and perhaps even the world. If you're reading this, I am either dead or in custody."I imagine the police will be the first to read this and seize it as evidence, so I will make something very clear. I made this decision to do so on my own."Another note read: "Am I evil for that? Probably. Am I an incel? A misogynist?. No. I just have good judgement."The trial continues.If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, you can visit the BBC Action Line for support and informationFollow Norfolk news on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, Instagram, external and X, external.

schema.headline: Stabbed Norwich schoolgirl went into 'panic mode', court told

title: Aleksander Ceferin to stand for fourth term as Uefa president
description: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin will stand for a fourth term as head of European football's governing body.Ceferin informed delegates of his decisio
body: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin will stand for a fourth term as head of European football's governing body.Ceferin informed delegates of his decision at a meeting of all 55 national association chiefs in Berlin.The move had been widely anticipated and reverses his insistence he would not seek re-election, which the Slovenian initially outlined in February 2024.At that point Ceferin, who was initially elected in 2016, was embroiled in a row over Uefa changing its statutes to allow him to serve for a fourth term.However, there had been a growing expectation the 58-year-old would stand.This has only been made more likely since Uefa launched its efforts to oust Fifa president Gianni Infantino, who scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors following widespread opposition.Ceferin has ruled out standing against Infantino himself but is committed to finding a candidate the game can unite around when Fifa holds its presidential election in March.

schema.headline: Aleksander Ceferin to stand for fourth term as Uefa president

title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
description: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the upda
body: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals.So too are the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.With this information, scammers may be able to craft potent phishing attack emails or phone calls.The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed."Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said. "We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached. Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action. But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity."Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio."Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information". "We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

schema.headline: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds

title: South Africa vs Australia: Pat Cummins speaks to Usman Khawaja about autobiography
description: Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about p
body: Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations.On Friday, Australia will begin their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering scandal erupted in Cape Town in 2018.At the time, captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were banned for their part in the plot.Since then, the four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including Cummins, have denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan to cheat.The quartet, who released a joint statement about the episode in 2021, are once again set to be united in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.Khawaja played in all four Tests in 2018 and retired from international cricket in January. His autobiography will be released in November."Uz gave me a buzz a few weeks back that he is releasing a book," said Cummins. "He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries."Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times."It was dealt with then and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on and we are very happy with the last eight to nine years how we have been as a group and evolved and obviously my focus is on captaining the cricket team."At the time of the ball-tampering controversy, Smith explained it was devised by the "leadership group" of the Australian team on the third day of the third Test in Cape Town. Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball the same day.While Smith, Warner and Bancroft – all batters – were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."Days after Bancroft's interview was published, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again."We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands."And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage."We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."Earlier this week, left-arm seamer Starc referenced the scandal when he said: "What's left to come out after eight years?"And, speaking on Thursday, Cummins said the episode was "a long time ago"."It's nothing new," the 33-year-old told ABC. "We've spoken about it a little bit. If the crowd gets rowdy or whatever, if someone needs an extra helping hand, we're around."To be honest, it's so long ago and we, as a group, move on from things pretty quickly. It hasn't taken up too much of our time."The trip to South Africa is the first in a year of high-profile away series for Australia. After what appears to be a stern challenge against New Zealand in their home summer, Cummins' men then travel to India and defend the Ashes in England next year.With all-rounder Cameron Green ruled out because of injury, the tourists are likely to choose between Cooper Connolly and Nic Maddinson for a place in the middle order.On a Durban pitch expected to turn, South Africa have included two spinners – Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer - in their XI.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Pat Cummins speaks to Usman Khawaja about autobiography

title: Super League: Wakefield top rankings as all 14 Super League clubs stay for 2027
description: All 14 Super League clubs will remain in the competition next season after the release of the yearly gradings, with Wakefield Trinity topping the rati
body: All 14 Super League clubs will remain in the competition next season after the release of the yearly gradings, with Wakefield Trinity topping the ratings for the first time.Following their Super League Grand Final success, Wakefield have come top of the ratings, based on criteria formulated by media giant IMG, with marks for five factors - fan experience, finance, stadium, community and on-field performance.London Broncos have come 16th on the list, below fellow Championship side Barrow Raiders, despite a season in which they won the second tier's Grand Final, the 1895 Cup and were runaway champions in the regular-season standings.The Broncos were overlooked 12 months ago when Bradford Bulls, York Knights and Toulouse Olympique joined the expanded 14-team competition.But, with the backing of Australian businessman Grant Wechsel, former Brisbane Broncos star Darren Lockyer and a squad full of internationals, they do still harbour hopes of playing in Super League in 2027.Australia's National Rugby League (NRL) is looking to invest in the competition, with talks at an advanced stage.It is understood any completed deal would involve the Australian governing body insisting on Broncos featuring in the top flight next season.Wakefield have matched 2025 champions Hull KR's record grading score of 17.85 from 12 months ago, to continue their rise on and off the field under Matt Ellis' ownership. In the same rankings last year they were eighth with a mark of 15.47, only just above the threshold for Category A status. "Wakefield Trinity's rise to the top of the 2026 club grading rankings is a fascinating story for rugby league, and a strong example of how sustained progress on and off the field can be recognised through the grading framework," said RFL chief executive Ian Nolan."Their achievement sits alongside encouraging movement across the sport, from growing attendances and digital audiences to continued improvements in facilities and community delivery."Leeds Rhinos remain second, although their score of 17.03 is slightly lower than they achieved in the 2025 rankings.Warrington Wolves have jumped from sixth to third on the back of a much stronger season which culminated in reaching the Grand Final at Old Trafford, only to lose to Wakefield.It is fourth place again for Wigan, who won both the Challenge Cup and the League Leaders' shield, just above Hull KR and Leigh Leopards. St Helens drop from third to seventh after a season in which they missed out on the play-offs for the first time in the Super League era.Castleford Tigers complete the Category A clubs as they have risen from 11th in 2025 to eighth and move into the top-tier section despite finishing 13th in Super League.Catalans Dragons and Hull FC are ninth and 10th, but both have fallen from an A to a B grade. Then come Bradford Bulls and Huddersfield Giants, with Toulouse Olympique and York Knights, occupying 13th and 14th, albeit with higher scores than last year.However, only six of the 14 Super League clubs have scored higher than they did 12 months ago.But there was a significant gap to the teams outside. York's score of 13.24 was comfortably higher than the next best, Barrow with 9.85, while London only achieved 9.77, which was down on their mark of 11.65 from last year.Overall, 26 clubs were graded on this system,, external split into three categories, A, B and C.

schema.headline: Super League: Wakefield top rankings as all 14 Super League clubs stay for 2027

title: Manchester City charges: Premier League clubs fear political interference in appeal after Andy Burnham comments
description: Senior club sources have said they found the comments "absolutely bizarre", and that it was "at best naive and at worst quite manipulative, and that i
body: Senior club sources have said they found the comments "absolutely bizarre", and that it was "at best naive and at worst quite manipulative, and that is not a good look".A different source said it was "clumsy", while another said they were surprised that the prime minister had "misspoken".The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with a sanctions hearing still to come. A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.However, when asked about potential interference in the process off the back of Burnham's comments, one senior club source said: "Everyone would have a degree of concern. How much would depend on how much you read into that comment. "I think everyone is concerned. Because no-one is stupid around the table. We understand the geopolitics as well. We understand the investment they have made in our country. I don't think anyone could doubt that or criticise that. But this is different, this is sport, this is our national game."Another club source, however, said the degree of scrutiny on Burnham now means they think any interference would be impossible.Burnham's comments came in an interview with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason the next day.When asked about 'Brand Manchester' taking a hit, the Prime Minister drew a parallel with a previous Premier League case with Everton, saying he still held the view "firmly" that they "weren't fairly treated".Everton were deducted 10 points, later reduced to six on appeal, by an independent commission for breaching Premier League financial rules.Asked if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them."They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city," he added.Burnham's comments provoked strong criticism.The following day, a No 10 spokesperson sought to clarify the comments, saying: "As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected."If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."However, this statement was amended following further criticism over the use of the word "if" - which was changed to "wherever".The Premier League is viewed by governments of different political stripes as one of the country's major cultural exports, so ministers are eager for the row not to cause lasting damage to its brand.Additionally, being a football fan is a core part of Burnham's political persona. He is an Everton season ticket holder and, prior to becoming prime minister, he spoke of hoping to continue sitting in his usual seat at Hill Dickinson Stadium - but this has not been possible because of security concerns, as was the case for Sir Keir Starmer, his Arsenal-supporting predecessor.Last month Burnham floated the prospect of lifting the ban on football fans drinking in the stands, though it was quickly clarified that this is not in fact government policy.

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Premier League clubs fear political interference in appeal after Andy Burnham comments
